function: Selects the broadcast (SSB) beam of each sector from a beam pool, maximizing RSRP coverage and limiting overlapping coverage (pp. 3-6).
system: 6 base stations, 18 sectors, each with a 12 x 8 FD-MIMO array (192 oscillators) and ZF precoding; no RIS; carrier frequency not stated (pp. 3, 8).
method: Multi-agent reinforcement learning: Q-learning with WoLF-PHC policy updates inside a moth-flame search, one agent per sector; offline training, then online retraining (pp. 5-8).
data_channel: China Mobile network grid and engineering data (14000 grids, 18 sectors, 148 beams); RSRP from a constructed free-space LoS/NLoS link model with shadow fading (pp. 3-4, 8-9, 12).
test_conditions: Trained offline once and tested on the same 18-sector area, one user per grid (uniform); only the beam-pool size varies, 20 to 140 beams (pp. 8-9, 12).
baselines: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) and moth-flame optimization (MFO), both non-learned swarm methods; no learned baseline (pp. 9-10).
metrics: RSRP coverage rate (grids above -85 dB), overlapping coverage rate, iterations to converge, and optimization time (pp. 1, 10-12).
complexity: Measured time per 1000 iterations on an Intel i5-10400 CPU, shown as coverage versus hours (Fig. 7); no complexity order or parameter count (pp. 8, 10).
openness: None: operator data from the China Mobile network, no code or data link given (p. 8).
q1_support: p. 3: "we constructed a wireless link model"; p. 4: "We set the free space propagation model as". The RSRP values come from this custom free-space link-budget model (LoS/NLoS, shadow fading, Table II on p. 8) laid on real network geometry. No 3GPP or other standard channel model is named, and the paper does not say the RSRP values were measured (p. 8: "the data comes from the China Mobile existing network").
q2_support: p. 8: "The experimental results are the results after training the model offline once." Evaluation is on the same grid dataset with uniform user density (p. 9: "one user on each grid"). Retraining on actual user density is described (p. 8) but no result in a new condition is reported; the sweep over 20 to 140 beams (p. 12) reruns each search and counts iterations.
q3_support: p. 10: "compare the optimization efficiency of the particle swarm algorithm, moth flame optimization algorithm, and MAMF-RL". Both baselines are non-learned swarm methods; no earlier learned method (for example DQN or the deep RL scheme of [28] cited on p. 2) is compared, so the learned-baseline condition is missing.
q4_support: p. 10: "we recorded the time spent by the algorithms for every 1000 iterations"; p. 11: "the proposed MAMF-RL requires the shortest convergence time". Fig. 7 (p. 10) plots RSRP coverage against measured time in hours for MAMF-RL, MFO and PSO on one CPU (p. 8); the text gives no numeric runtime and no complexity order.
q5_support: p. 8: "the data comes from the China Mobile existing network". The paper gives no link, DOI or code statement anywhere; the grid RSRP values are produced by the constructed link model (p. 3), so the data are neither public nor stated as measured.
notes: Area 3 reading: coverage-oriented selection of the SSB broadcast beam of each sector from a fixed pool of 148 beams on a 192-oscillator array (pp. 3, 8, 12); counted as beams of area 3, not antenna hardware design and not user-level precoding. Learned element: Q-learning with WoLF-PHC policy updates that replace the spiral move of moth-flame optimization (pp. 5-7); counted as reinforcement learning. REVIEWER CHECK for q1 and q5: the abstract (p. 1) says "utilizing real data" and p. 8 says the data come from the China Mobile existing network, but p. 3 says the grid RSRP values were generated with a constructed wireless link model; if the grid RSRP table is read as measured data, q1 and q5 would be 1. q4 rests on the runtime that is shown only in Fig. 7 (p. 10) and described in the text of pp. 10-11.
